Conducted by researchers from Columbia University and the Zambia Ministry of Health, the investigation utilized an individual-based transmission model calibrated to national demographic records, local sexual partnership dynamics, and empirical epidemiological data. The primary findings establish that while routine vaccination of pre-adolescent girls serves as a vital cornerstone for long-term control, immunization alone produces minimal epidemiological impact during the initial twenty years of implementation because existing disease burdens reside almost exclusively among adult cohorts who remain unimmunized. By contrast, pairing school-based vaccination programs with an expansive molecular screening campaign capable of administering approximately 400,000 tests annually accelerates clinical gains dramatically, averting an estimated 34,000 cervical cancer cases by 2040 and more than 183,000 cumulative cases by 2060. Zambia currently confronts one of the highest cervical cancer burdens documented worldwide, characterized in 2020 by an estimated crude annual incidence of 34.1 cases per 100,000 women and an associated mortality rate of 20.5 per 100,000 women, corresponding to an observed case fatality ratio of roughly 60 percent. This public health crisis is intensified by exceptionally high baseline exposure to high-risk viral strains, with a 2022 national population survey indicating that approximately 30 percent of women aged 25 to 49 test positive for oncogenic human papillomavirus. The transmission dynamic is further compounded by the concurrent human immunodeficiency virus epidemic, where an estimated 14.2 percent of Zambian women aged 15 to 49 live with HIV. Zambia introduced visual inspection with acetic acid within HIV clinics in 2006 and initiated a national single-dose vaccination campaign for girls aged 9 to 14 in 2019, yet structural access barriers across rural territories have continually constrained diagnostic coverage. Under this collaborative framework designed by ICAP at Columbia University and the Zambia Ministry of Health, rural community health volunteers facilitate patient self-collection of vaginal specimens, which undergo rapid automated testing using portable battery-powered molecular equipment capable of delivering high-performance DNA results equivalent to provider-collected samples. Expanding this molecular see-and-treat protocol beyond HIV-dedicated settings to all women aged 25 to 49 establishes a practical programmatic mechanism to bypass facility deficits and extend effective secondary prevention across remote populations. Discover more Find Cancer Care See an OB-GYN cancer Cancer To rigorously evaluate the population-level consequences of this expanded diagnostic delivery model, the investigators constructed an individual-based computational model that simulated transmission mechanics and disease natural history across 50,000 synthetic individuals initialized from Zambia’s 2019 age and sex distribution. Demographic projections incorporated empirical survival schedules, age-stratified birth rates, and historical census data compiled by the United States Census Bureau. The computational architecture simulated annual time steps wherein individuals entered the sexually active population upon reaching age 15. Annual partnership formation was governed by Poisson distributions reflecting age-specific mean partnership frequencies derived from sub-Saharan African behavioral datasets, with mixing constrained to opposite-sex partnerships within a five-year age difference to mirror documented national marital age gaps. The model accounted for changing human immunodeficiency virus background dynamics by holding adult HIV incidence fixed at 0.31 percent overall, reflecting calibrated 2021 national survey findings, while assigning risk ratios to represent accelerated infection and progression rates among immunocompromised women receiving modern antiretroviral therapy. The biological natural history within the model tracked individual infection longevity across discrete disease compartments: uninfected susceptibility, active oncogenic infection, aggregated precancerous cervical lesion, invasive cancer, and cause-specific mortality. Drawing on established biological trajectories, the authors specified that 85 percent of newly acquired infections clear spontaneously within four years without inducing permanent tissue dysplasia. For individuals experiencing persistent infection, transition probabilities governed progression into an aggregated lesion state, where lesions were required to persist for a mandatory dwell time of at least five years before becoming capable of advancing to invasive malignancy. Model calibration aligned parameters against observed empirical benchmarks, identifying a calibrated cumulative progression probability of 0.30 from persistent lesion to cancer, an annual infection-to-lesion transition rate of 0.012, a median progression interval from viral acquisition to invasive disease of 27 years, and a median age at cancer presentation of 46 years, matching observed clinical profiles in southern Africa. Discover more Check Symptoms Book a Checkup Book Lab Tests Using these calibrated baseline parameters, the research team projected Zambian disease trajectories through 2064 across five standardized counterfactual scenarios to contrast isolated interventions against integrated programmatic scale-up. The reference counterfactual, designated as No Interventions, modeled the complete withdrawal of national testing and vaccination activities after 2024, causing projected cervical cancer incidence to climb from 34 cases per 100,000 women in 2020 to 49 cases per 100,000 by 2060 as population aging expanded the demographic pool of mature adult women. The second scenario, Vaccination Only, sustained a constant 73 percent single-dose coverage rate among girls aged 9 to 14 with an assumed lifelong vaccine efficacy of 90 percent, but discontinued secondary screening. The third scenario preserved ongoing visual inspection with acetic acid starting at 154,280 annual tests and expanding by 5 percent annually while maintaining historical prioritization for women living with HIV. The fourth and fifth scenarios modeled universal molecular screening for all women aged 25 to 49, initiating testing volumes at 200,000 and 400,000 molecular tests per year respectively, both incorporating annual 5 percent expansion. Analysis of the simulation trajectories showed that relying exclusively on adolescent immunization leaves national cancer rates largely unaffected for multiple decades. Under the Vaccination Only pathway, cervical cancer incidence declined by an imperceptible 3.4 percent over the initial twenty years through 2040, because vaccinated adolescents required decades to age into the peak demographic windows of oncogenic vulnerability. Although isolated immunization eventually yielded a 29 percent reduction in annual cancer incidence by 2050 and a 47 percent reduction by 2060, it averted only 1,000 cumulative cancer cases during the first twenty years and 57,000 cumulative cases across the full forty-year horizon. Continuing traditional visual inspection with acetic acid produced intermediate outcomes, achieving a modest 14 percent incidence reduction by 2040 and a 61 percent reduction by 2060, while averting 80,000 cumulative malignancies over forty years. The visual approach was constrained by lower operator-dependent diagnostic sensitivity, documented between 22.8 percent and 48 percent in Zambian clinical evaluations, and structural reliance on clinical examination rooms. Universal population screening utilizing molecular DNA assays yielded dramatic, immediate reductions in disease incidence, fundamentally outperforming visual triage. Expanding molecular testing capacity to 200,000 tests annually achieved a 40 percent decline in cervical cancer incidence within twenty years and an 88 percent reduction after forty years, averting more than 143,000 cumulative cases by 2060. Increasing molecular throughput to 400,000 annual tests reduced national incidence by 64 percent by 2040 and 97 percent by 2060, bringing crude incidence down to approximately 2 cases per 100,000 women. Furthermore, the 400,000 annual test scenario satisfied the global target of maintaining 70 percent of adult women up to date with screening guidelines by 2032, averting 34,000 incident malignancies by 2040, 94,000 by 2050, and 183,000 cumulative cases by 2060, while preventing over 18,000 premature deaths. In secondary exploratory analyses simulating eighty-year transmission dynamics across varying vaccination coverage levels without concurrent screening, the researchers examined the indirect herd protection conferred by extending human papillomavirus vaccination to school-aged boys. At low to intermediate coverage levels, adding boys to national immunization registers produced substantial secondary protection for women. Specifically, achieving 37 percent coverage among both sexes prevented more than 120,000 additional cervical cancer cases over eighty years compared to immunizing 37 percent of eligible females alone, demonstrating how male immunization suppresses circulating viral transmission throughout shared sexual networks. However, the marginal epidemiological benefit of male vaccination diminished sharply as female immunization rates reached higher thresholds; under a hypothetical 91 percent female coverage scenario, expanding coverage to boys yielded only 4,387 additional averted cases across eighty years. These findings indicate that while universal sex-neutral immunization offers an effective mechanism to bolster herd immunity when female uptake is constrained by social hesitancy or delivery logistics, prioritizing universal coverage among girls remains the most efficient allocation of constrained resources. The authors highlighted several critical methodological assumptions and real-world operational challenges that contextualize their projections. The mathematical architecture utilized an aggregated lesion compartment rather than differentiating specific histological grades of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, and partnership formation relied on annual stochastic resampling rather than dynamic long-term partnership tracking. Moreover, while baseline projections incorporated an optimistic 73 percent female vaccination coverage rate, actual Zambian adolescent uptake dropped from 99 percent in 2019 to 44 percent in 2021 before recovering to an estimated 52 percent by 2025. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health HPV-Positive Head And Neck Cancers Show Higher PD-L1 Levels In Cross-Sectional Study by November 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 HPV-Positive Head And Neck Cancers Show Higher PD-L1 Levels In Cross-Sectional Study Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In an ambispective cross-sectional evaluation of 100 patients with histopathologically confirmed head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, tumors testing positive for human papillomavirus DNA demonstrated a significantly higher frequency of programmed death ligand-1 expression compared to HPV DNA-negative cases. The study, conducted at Government Medical College in Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh, India, identified PD-L1 positivity in 73.8 percent of HPV DNA-positive tumors compared with 53.4 percent of HPV DNA-negative specimens. This observation corresponded to an odds ratio of 2.45, indicating that the odds of expressing PD-L1 were more than twice as high among HPV DNA-positive malignant tissues. However, the investigators noted that because of the cross-sectional investigation framework, these findings represent an exploratory association rather than proof of biological causality, clinical prognosis, or direct therapeutic responsiveness. At the same time, overall PD-L1 expression across the entire unstratified patient cohort reached 62 percent, aligning broadly with previously reported literature rates. Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma represents a substantial global healthcare burden characterized by pronounced morbidity and mortality. The disease encompasses malignancies originating within the mucosal epithelium of the oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx, with squamous cell carcinoma accounting for more than 90 percent of all diagnosed cases. Despite continuous advancements in surgical interventions, radiotherapy schedules, and cytotoxic chemotherapy regimens, the overall five-year survival rate for affected individuals remains approximately 50 percent, largely driven by late clinical presentation, aggressive local recurrence, and distant metastatic dissemination. Historically, regular tobacco consumption and persistent alcohol use have served as the primary epidemiological risk factors driving neoplastic transformation. Over recent decades, however, persistent oncogenic infection with human papillomavirus, particularly high-risk genotype HPV-16, has emerged as an increasingly prominent etiological contributor, especially within the oropharynx. HPV-positive head and neck malignancies form a clinically distinct pathological subset characterized by improved therapeutic responsiveness and superior overall survival rates. Within cancer research, the interaction between tumor cells and the surrounding immune microenvironment has become a central focus for understanding immune evasion mechanisms. The biological axis formed by programmed death-1 and programmed death ligand-1 operates as an essential immune checkpoint pathway, wherein PD-L1 displayed on neoplastic cells and tumor-infiltrating immune cells binds to PD-1 receptors present on cytotoxic T lymphocytes. This binding event inhibits downstream T-cell activation, blunting antitumor immune responses and permitting neoplastic cells to escape surveillance. Aberrant overexpression of PD-L1 occurs across numerous human malignancies, including head and neck carcinomas, where it correlates with local progression and localized immune suppression. The clinical introduction of checkpoint inhibitors targeting this pathway, such as the monoclonal antibodies pembrolizumab and nivolumab, has provided demonstrable therapeutic efficacy in recurrent and metastatic head and neck cancers. Nevertheless, the predictive reliability of PD-L1 assessment remains variable across clinical trials due to marked intratumoral heterogeneity and methodological differences. Discover more Find Cancer Care cancers Cancers cancer Check Symptoms The study evaluated a hospital-based cohort of 100 histopathologically confirmed primary head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cases collected over an 18-month observational timeline. The patient population ranged from 35 to 75 years of age, with a cohort mean age of 56 years and a standard deviation of 10 years, concentrating primarily in the fifth and sixth decades of life. Demographic assessment revealed a notable male predominance consisting of 72 male patients and 28 female patients, yielding a male-to-female ratio of 2.6 to 1. Tobacco usage was documented in 68 percent of participants, while 52 percent reported routine alcohol intake. Topographically, the oral cavity represented the most frequent primary tumor site, followed by the oropharynx, larynx, and other localized anatomical regions. Pathological TNM staging classified 38 cases as early-stage disease, comprising stages I and II, while 62 cases presented with advanced-stage disease, spanning stages III and IV. Histological differentiation revealed 24 well-differentiated tumors, 52 moderately differentiated tumors, and 24 poorly differentiated tumors. Conducted as an ambispective observational investigation, the study incorporated both archival formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue blocks and prospectively accrued primary surgical specimens following formal Institutional Ethics Committee approval granted on August 12, 2024. Prospectively enrolled patients provided written informed consent prior to tissue acquisition, whereas retrospective cases were evaluated using anonymized archival records meeting rigorous preservation criteria. The authors applied strict eligibility boundaries: only primary tumor specimens were analyzed, explicitly excluding recurrent lesions, metastatic deposits, and cases with prior exposure to neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Specimens demonstrating compromised tissue integrity, insufficient tumor volume, incomplete clinical records, or missing essential laboratory data were excluded from downstream analysis. All qualified tissue specimens were fixed using standard 10 percent neutral buffered formalin, routinely processed through histological cassettes, and embedded in paraffin blocks. Serial microtome sections cut at three to four micrometers were stained with hematoxylin and eosin to confirm diagnosis and grade. Laboratory evaluations of PD-L1 expression were outsourced to an external accredited diagnostic facility utilizing validated automated immunohistochemical protocols. Staining was conducted on serial formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded sections of three to four micrometers mounted on positively charged glass slides using the primary anti-PD-L1 antibody clone CAL10 manufactured by Biocare Medical. Deparaffinization, rehydration, and heat-induced epitope retrieval using an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid buffer at pH 9.0 were executed on an automated Ventana BenchMark platform from Roche Diagnostics. Endogenous peroxidase activity was chemically blocked prior to primary antibody incubation, and visualization was achieved using a polymer-based horseradish peroxidase detection system paired with diaminobenzidine chromogen and hematoxylin counterstaining without signal amplification. Formalin-fixed human tonsil tissue served as an external positive control, while negative controls omitted the primary antibody. Scoring utilized the Combined Positive Score, calculated as the absolute number of PD-L1-staining tumor cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages divided by total viable tumor cells, multiplied by 100, defining positivity as a score of one or greater. Microscopic evaluation of PD-L1 expression across all 100 head and neck squamous cell carcinoma specimens demonstrated positive staining in 62 cases, representing an overall positivity rate of 62 percent, while 38 cases demonstrated an absence of PD-L1 expression. Stratification across four mutually exclusive Combined Positive Score intervals revealed that 38 specimens exhibited a score below one, 24 specimens fell into the low-expression bracket ranging from one to nine, 16 specimens occupied the intermediate category spanning scores from 10 to 19, and 22 specimens demonstrated high expression with scores equal to or exceeding 20. Staining patterns were characterized by convincing membranous positivity along neoplastic cell borders alongside cytoplasmic or membranous staining within stromal immune infiltrates. The observed 62 percent overall positivity rate falls directly within the broad 46 percent to 92 percent range previously documented in published head and neck cancer literature. Statistical correlation analyses demonstrated that PD-L1 positivity did not significantly associate with patient age, sex, tumor anatomical site, histological differentiation, clinical stage, or lymph node metastasis. Evaluation of human papillomavirus status commenced with automated DNA testing using the cobas HPV platform on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor sections. The cobas assay individually discriminates high-risk genotypes HPV-16 and HPV-18 while simultaneously screening for a pooled group of 12 other high-risk genotypes, including HPV-31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, and 68. Across the cohort, 42 cases tested positive for HPV DNA, while 58 cases were negative. Among the 42 positive cases, genotype HPV-16 accounted for 34 cases, whereas the remaining eight cases harbored other pooled high-risk genotypes. Topographical distribution demonstrated a statistically significant association with anatomical tumor site, where the oropharynx exhibited the highest infection frequency at 71.4 percent, representing 20 positive cases out of 28 tumors. Furthermore, HPV DNA positivity correlated significantly with histological differentiation: poorly differentiated carcinomas demonstrated a 70.8 percent positivity rate, compared with 38.5 percent in moderately differentiated tumors and 20.8 percent in well-differentiated tumors, reflecting characteristic viral morphologic patterns. To verify transcriptional viral activity beyond mere viral DNA presence, researchers performed RNA in situ hybridization utilizing the RNAscope 2.5 HD Reagent Kit with probes directed against high-risk HPV E6/E7 messenger RNA transcripts. Positive expression was recognized by punctate brown hybridization signals within the nuclei or cytoplasm of viable tumor cells. Comparative concordance analysis between cobas DNA testing and RNA in situ hybridization demonstrated strong diagnostic agreement across 95 of the 100 examined cases, yielding an overall concordance rate of 95.0 percent. Among the 42 cobas DNA-positive tumors, 39 showed concordant positive E6/E7 mRNA signals, while three tumors lacked detectable transcripts. Conversely, among 58 DNA-negative tumors, 56 were concordantly negative, and two exhibited positive mRNA hybridization. Statistical evaluation yielded a Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.89, establishing robust concordance between automated DNA detection and transcriptionally active messenger RNA identification. The authors emphasized that reserving the term HPV-associated disease for transcriptionally active, mRNA-confirmed cases prevents clinical misclassification arising from transient non-transcriptionally active viral colonization. Cross-tabulation of biomarker expression revealed that 31 of 42 HPV DNA-positive tumors expressed PD-L1 compared with 31 of 58 HPV DNA-negative tumors, confirming a statistically significant correlation with an odds ratio of 2.45. This observation supports the hypothesis that HPV-positive head and neck tumors frequently foster an immune-active microenvironment characterized by adaptive PD-L1 upregulation. Nonetheless, the authors outlined critical limitations governing their investigation. The cross-sectional design restricts analysis to observational associations, precluding inferences regarding biological causality, long-term survival, or therapeutic responsiveness. Furthermore, immunohistochemical assessment utilized the CAL10 antibody clone rather than an officially validated companion diagnostic assay, meaning these measurements cannot establish direct eligibility for therapeutic checkpoint inhibition. Additionally, the presence of discordant findings between DNA and RNA platforms underscores the necessity of standardizing molecular definitions for HPV status. Consequently, the authors concluded that these exploratory findings warrant validation through larger multicentric investigations incorporating standardized diagnostic assays, uniform testing algorithms, and longitudinal clinical outcome monitoring. Nevertheless, the predictive reliability of PD-L1 assessment remains variable across clinical trials due to marked intratumoral heterogeneity and methodological differences. Discover more Find Cancer Care cancers Cancers cancer Check Symptoms The study evaluated a hospital-based cohort of 100 histopathologically confirmed primary head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cases collected over an 18-month observational timeline. The patient population ranged from 35 to 75 years of age, with a cohort mean age of 56 years and a standard deviation of 10 years, concentrating primarily in the fifth and sixth decades of life. Demographic assessment revealed a notable male predominance consisting of 72 male patients and 28 female patients, yielding a male-to-female ratio of 2.6 to 1. Tobacco usage was documented in 68 percent of participants, while 52 percent reported routine alcohol intake. Topographically, the oral cavity represented the most frequent primary tumor site, followed by the oropharynx, larynx, and other localized anatomical regions. Pathological TNM staging classified 38 cases as early-stage disease, comprising stages I and II, while 62 cases presented with advanced-stage disease, spanning stages III and IV. Histological differentiation revealed 24 well-differentiated tumors, 52 moderately differentiated tumors, and 24 poorly differentiated tumors. Conducted as an ambispective observational investigation, the study incorporated both archival formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue blocks and prospectively accrued primary surgical specimens following formal Institutional Ethics Committee approval granted on August 12, 2024. Prospectively enrolled patients provided written informed consent prior to tissue acquisition, whereas retrospective cases were evaluated using anonymized archival records meeting rigorous preservation criteria. The authors applied strict eligibility boundaries: only primary tumor specimens were analyzed, explicitly excluding recurrent lesions, metastatic deposits, and cases with prior exposure to neoadjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Specimens demonstrating compromised tissue integrity, insufficient tumor volume, incomplete clinical records, or missing essential laboratory data were excluded from downstream analysis. All qualified tissue specimens were fixed using standard 10 percent neutral buffered formalin, routinely processed through histological cassettes, and embedded in paraffin blocks. Serial microtome sections cut at three to four micrometers were stained with hematoxylin and eosin to confirm diagnosis and grade. Laboratory evaluations of PD-L1 expression were outsourced to an external accredited diagnostic facility utilizing validated automated immunohistochemical protocols. Staining was conducted on serial formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded sections of three to four micrometers mounted on positively charged glass slides using the primary anti-PD-L1 antibody clone CAL10 manufactured by Biocare Medical. Deparaffinization, rehydration, and heat-induced epitope retrieval using an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid buffer at pH 9.0 were executed on an automated Ventana BenchMark platform from Roche Diagnostics. Endogenous peroxidase activity was chemically blocked prior to primary antibody incubation, and visualization was achieved using a polymer-based horseradish peroxidase detection system paired with diaminobenzidine chromogen and hematoxylin counterstaining without signal amplification. Formalin-fixed human tonsil tissue served as an external positive control, while negative controls omitted the primary antibody. Scoring utilized the Combined Positive Score, calculated as the absolute number of PD-L1-staining tumor cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages divided by total viable tumor cells, multiplied by 100, defining positivity as a score of one or greater. Microscopic evaluation of PD-L1 expression across all 100 head and neck squamous cell carcinoma specimens demonstrated positive staining in 62 cases, representing an overall positivity rate of 62 percent, while 38 cases demonstrated an absence of PD-L1 expression. Stratification across four mutually exclusive Combined Positive Score intervals revealed that 38 specimens exhibited a score below one, 24 specimens fell into the low-expression bracket ranging from one to nine, 16 specimens occupied the intermediate category spanning scores from 10 to 19, and 22 specimens demonstrated high expression with scores equal to or exceeding 20. Staining patterns were characterized by convincing membranous positivity along neoplastic cell borders alongside cytoplasmic or membranous staining within stromal immune infiltrates. The observed 62 percent overall positivity rate falls directly within the broad 46 percent to 92 percent range previously documented in published head and neck cancer literature. Statistical correlation analyses demonstrated that PD-L1 positivity did not significantly associate with patient age, sex, tumor anatomical site, histological differentiation, clinical stage, or lymph node metastasis. Evaluation of human papillomavirus status commenced with automated DNA testing using the cobas HPV platform on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor sections. The cobas assay individually discriminates high-risk genotypes HPV-16 and HPV-18 while simultaneously screening for a pooled group of 12 other high-risk genotypes, including HPV-31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, and 68. Across the cohort, 42 cases tested positive for HPV DNA, while 58 cases were negative. Among the 42 positive cases, genotype HPV-16 accounted for 34 cases, whereas the remaining eight cases harbored other pooled high-risk genotypes. Topographical distribution demonstrated a statistically significant association with anatomical tumor site, where the oropharynx exhibited the highest infection frequency at 71.4 percent, representing 20 positive cases out of 28 tumors. Furthermore, HPV DNA positivity correlated significantly with histological differentiation: poorly differentiated carcinomas demonstrated a 70.8 percent positivity rate, compared with 38.5 percent in moderately differentiated tumors and 20.8 percent in well-differentiated tumors, reflecting characteristic viral morphologic patterns. To verify transcriptional viral activity beyond mere viral DNA presence, researchers performed RNA in situ hybridization utilizing the RNAscope 2.5 HD Reagent Kit with probes directed against high-risk HPV E6/E7 messenger RNA transcripts. Positive expression was recognized by punctate brown hybridization signals within the nuclei or cytoplasm of viable tumor cells. Comparative concordance analysis between cobas DNA testing and RNA in situ hybridization demonstrated strong diagnostic agreement across 95 of the 100 examined cases, yielding an overall concordance rate of 95.0 percent. Among the 42 cobas DNA-positive tumors, 39 showed concordant positive E6/E7 mRNA signals, while three tumors lacked detectable transcripts. Conversely, among 58 DNA-negative tumors, 56 were concordantly negative, and two exhibited positive mRNA hybridization. Statistical evaluation yielded a Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.89, establishing robust concordance between automated DNA detection and transcriptionally active messenger RNA identification. The authors emphasized that reserving the term HPV-associated disease for transcriptionally active, mRNA-confirmed cases prevents clinical misclassification arising from transient non-transcriptionally active viral colonization. Cross-tabulation of biomarker expression revealed that 31 of 42 HPV DNA-positive tumors expressed PD-L1 compared with 31 of 58 HPV DNA-negative tumors, confirming a statistically significant correlation with an odds ratio of 2.45. This observation supports the hypothesis that HPV-positive head and neck tumors frequently foster an immune-active microenvironment characterized by adaptive PD-L1 upregulation. Nonetheless, the authors outlined critical limitations governing their investigation. The cross-sectional design restricts analysis to observational associations, precluding inferences regarding biological causality, long-term survival, or therapeutic responsiveness. Furthermore, immunohistochemical assessment utilized the CAL10 antibody clone rather than an officially validated companion diagnostic assay, meaning these measurements cannot establish direct eligibility for therapeutic checkpoint inhibition. Additionally, the presence of discordant findings between DNA and RNA platforms underscores the necessity of standardizing molecular definitions for HPV status. Consequently, the authors concluded that these exploratory findings warrant validation through larger multicentric investigations incorporating standardized diagnostic assays, uniform testing algorithms, and longitudinal clinical outcome monitoring. 人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)相关头颈癌(HNCs),尤其是口咽鳞状细胞癌(OPSCC),构成日益加重的全球健康负担,近几十年来发病率快速上升。此类肿瘤在生物学和临床上不同于HPV阴性HNCs,更常见于传统危险因素如烟草和酒精暴露有限的年轻个体。HPV驱动的致癌过程由病毒癌蛋白E6和E7介导,其通过使p53和视网膜母细胞瘤(Rb)通路失活破坏基因组稳定性,促进不受控制的增殖、基因组不稳定和治疗耐药。当前HPV阳性HNCs的治疗策略包括手术、放疗和化疗,以顺铂为基础的放化疗(CRT)仍是局部晚期疾病的标准治疗。然而,HPV阳性患者治疗反应和总体预后改善,促使研究人员关注在不损害疗效的前提下降低毒性的治疗降阶梯策略。微创手术方法,如经口机器人手术(TORS),以及降低强度的放疗方案显示出有前景的功能学结局。免疫治疗是复发和转移性疾病的重要进展,靶向PD-1/PD-L1轴的免疫检查点抑制剂在选定患者群体中显示生存获益。新兴方法包括针对HPV癌蛋白的治疗性疫苗、过继性T细胞转移、靶向治疗、溶瘤病毒治疗,以及旨在沉默E6/E7表达或恢复抑癌功能的基因治疗。纳米医学进一步为药物递送、放射增敏和免疫调节提供新平台,提高治疗特异性和疗效。尽管取得显著进展,重大挑战仍然存在,包括早期诊断的限制、治疗耐药、生物标志物驱动的患者选择以及公众对HPV相关癌症风险认识不足。整合先进诊断方法,如循环肿瘤HPV DNA检测和下一代测序(NGS),可能改善风险分层和治疗监测。持续研究联合治疗、靶向方法和患者定制治疗算法对于改善结局仍至关重要。总之,HPV相关HNCs不断演变的治疗策略反映了向精准肿瘤学的转变,重点关注改善生存、降低毒性以及由分子肿瘤特征驱动的个体化干预。 引言:HNCs传统上与吸烟和饮酒相关,但HPV日益成为尤其口咽部恶性肿瘤的重要病因。HPV可经口交、深吻、自体接种和垂直传播;性行为变化和烟草使用下降可能促成HPV相关HNC发病率上升。疾病可在感染后长达40年出现,患者常较年轻、健康且缺乏典型危险因素,导致诊断延迟。HPV阳性HNSCC通常生存优于阴性,但高HPV整合等亚组预后较差。HNC约90%为鳞状细胞癌,2022年全球约74.5万新病例;近几十年HPV相关HNSCC全球发病率增加36.5%,约25% HNC归因于HPV,口咽癌30.8%、喉癌2.4%、口腔癌2.2%;多数与HPV 16/18相关,疫苗是最有效预防手段并应覆盖男性。OPSCC风险分层由NCCN和ESMO共识标准化。本文整合最新降阶梯试验(包括NRG-HN005、ORATOR2、PATHOS)、当前指南推荐、免疫检查点抑制剂更新指征和新兴方法,并评价证据水平与实施障碍。 HPV相关HNCs的流行病学:全球HPV每年导致63万新癌症病例,占4.5%;酒精约5%、烟草34%、二者合并36%的HNC。HPV相关HNSCC发病率上升,危险因素和人口学特征不同于HPV阴性者。HPV相关HNSCC主要发生于口咽,HPV在其他头颈部位因果作用较弱;欧洲新发和死亡数高于美国。HPV阴性HNC多见于老年、社会经济地位较低和口腔卫生差者;HPV阳性者常较年轻(45–64岁)、非吸烟、无明显饮酒史,多个性伴侣尤其口交史为危险因素;男性风险为女性2–4倍,且存在种族差异。分子上HPV阳性肿瘤表达E6/E7并使p53和pRb失活;HPV阴性HNSCC常见TP53和细胞周期调控改变,预后较差。HPV阳性OPSCC放化疗反应和预后优于阴性;HPV在宫颈鳞状细胞癌(CSCC)和OPSCC均关键,但OPSCC放射敏感性更高,口咽局部免疫反应更强,HPV特异性T细胞浸润更多、调节性T细胞(Treg)活性更低。 HPV在癌症发生中的病理机制:WHO将14型HPV列为致癌型。HPV为DNA病毒,嗜鳞状上皮,微损伤使致癌型HPV感染基底上皮干细胞,潜在受体包括整合素α-6、层粘连蛋白-332和硫酸类肝素蛋白聚糖。E1/E2支持病毒复制和附加体维持;E5、E6、E7促进细胞周期进展并抑制凋亡,E4与G2阻滞相关;上层上皮表达L1/L2并组装释放病毒。病毒整合可致突变和染色体异常。HPV通过调节细胞周期、干扰DNA修复、诱导氧化应激和改变端粒长度诱导基因组不稳定;E6促进人端粒酶逆转录酶(hTERT)转录并增加端粒酶活性,延长增殖并延迟衰老。E6结合p53并促其蛋白酶体降解;E7结合pRb使其失活,释放E2F,促进细胞周期基因表达,并可致染色体复制错误和纺锤体异常。E7作为致癌应激激活p53和p16INK4A反应,但E6通过E6相关蛋白(E6AP)介导的泛素-蛋白酶体途径降解p53以抵消保护;二者协同促进永生化与恶性转化。耐药机制包括E6抑制凋亡、E7促进增殖、细胞周期和DNA修复紊乱、干扰Toll样受体(TLRs)等模式识别受体(PRRs)逃避先天免疫、激活DNA损伤反应和修复(DDR)通路,以及缺氧、细胞外基质(ECM)重塑和基质细胞相互作用形成保护性微环境。 HPV相关HNCs的当前治疗策略:历史上HPV阳性和阴性HNSCC治疗相同。局部晚期标准为顺铂为基础CRT,使用70–72 Gy调强放疗(IMRT);单纯放疗用于早期或降阶梯方案。NCCN和EHNS-ESMO-ESTRO将p16阳性口咽癌视为独立实体,AJCC第8版有独立分期;早期推荐根治性放疗或经口手术加颈清扫,局部晚期仍以顺铂为基础CRT为标准;术后结外侵犯或切缘阳性需辅助放疗或放化疗;不推荐西妥昔单抗替代顺铂,临床试验外降阶梯为研究性;复发/转移一线首选依据PD-L1联合阳性评分(CPS)选择的帕博利珠单抗方案。降阶梯试验未证明肿瘤学安全性:RTOG 1016和De-ESCALaTE中西妥昔单抗替代顺铂结局较差且未降低毒性;NRG-HN005中标准CRT 2年无进展生存(PFS)98.1%,减量放疗加顺铂88.6%、加纳武利尤单抗90.3%,均未达非劣效;ORATOR2因手术组两例治疗相关死亡提前终止,2年总生存(OS)放疗100% vs 手术90%,PFS 100% vs 86%。PATHOS相关队列显示TORS后鼻胃管依赖高于经口激光显微手术(TLM)(45.0% vs 7.9%)。TORS在T1–T2且无需辅助治疗时功能获益较明显,需辅助治疗时优势大多消失;TORS加选择性颈清扫(SND)与广泛手术生存相当。IMRT需准确靶区勾画,PET-CT可改变分期和靶区覆盖但缺乏生存和HPV特异性证据;3D打印证据限于小型回顾性系列。复发/转移以铂类联合吉西他滨和顺铂为一线,但疗效有限、毒性高,促使研究新辅助、减量放疗和手术先行。免疫治疗中纳武利尤单抗和帕博利珠单抗靶向PD-1/PD-L1,已用于铂类失败后及一线PD-L1阳性(CPS≥1)或联合铂类和5-氟尿嘧啶;围手术期帕博利珠单抗用于可切除局部晚期HNSCC且CPS≥1。HPV状态不预测免疫治疗获益,单药缓解率约13–19%,获益主要由PD-L1表达决定。治疗性疫苗ISA-101、MEDI0457、PDS0101靶向E6/E7并联合PD-1阻断;过继T细胞转移和工程化TCR在早期研究。NGS可检测PIK3CA、TP53、NOTCH1和表观遗传改变;微滴数字PCR(ddPCR)和循环肿瘤DNA(ctDNA)液体活检用于无创监测。APG-157和组织驻留自然杀伤细胞(trNK)亚群trNK-1等为探索性方向。 新兴治疗策略:许多方法主要由临床前数据支持,细胞系和动物模型不能完全再现人类肿瘤复杂性,需适当期临床试验确认。循环肿瘤HPV DNA(ctHPV DNA)是最有前景的液体活检之一,ddPCR和NGS可检测根治后微小残留病(MRD),可早于影像3–6个月提示复发,但需前瞻多中心验证、标准化方法和截断值。降阶梯旨在减少副作用并保留疗效,策略包括省略化疗、降低或省略放疗,可保留咽喉功能、减少长期毒性、改善生活质量。免疫检查点抑制剂是重要方向,帕博利珠单抗和纳武利尤单抗阻断PD-1/PD-L1,在复发/转移中有效,研究单用或与放化疗联合。靶向治疗包括表皮生长因子受体(EGFR)抑制剂、mTOR和PI3K/Akt通路抑制剂;PI3K抑制剂耐药可被胰岛素样生长因子1受体(IGF1R)抑制剂克服;阿法替尼抑制多个HER受体。溶瘤病毒如T-Vec和Reolysin选择性破坏癌细胞并刺激免疫,在临床试验中与检查点抑制剂联合有潜力。光动力治疗(PDT)用于早期癌症和癌前病变。基因治疗用RNAi、siRNA或shRNA沉默E6/E7;免疫原性基因治疗引入HPV抗原基因;恢复抑癌功能的基因编辑处于实验阶段。纳米颗粒可靶向递送药物、检查点抑制剂和放射增敏剂,降低全身毒性;纳米疫苗如四价纳米疫苗和Qbeta-HPVag在临床前模型增强树突细胞和T细胞活化;ISA101联合纳武利尤单抗II期客观缓解率(ORR)33%、中位OS 17.5个月;磁性纳米颗粒热疗主要在临床前评估。 HPV相关HNCs管理中的挑战:临床评估仍主要依赖侵入性方法,可能延迟诊断;ctHPV DNA液体活检精确但费用高、缺乏标准化。罕见亚型分类需专家病理复核,回顾研究中半数病例复核后重新分类、16%存在重大差异。公众认识不足,调查仅30.6%了解HPV、29.2%将其与口咽癌联系。唾液HPV16 E6/E7检测对p16阳性肿瘤灵敏度72%–77%、特异度90%–94%,但受设备和人员限制。数字健康技术可远程监测症状、体重、营养和毒性,但缺乏HPV相关HNC证据,数据安全和成本待解决。约20–25%HPV阳性HNSCC复发,与肿瘤异质性、免疫逃逸和癌症干细胞样细胞有关;复发癌可见HPV基因活性和染色质结构改变。免疫治疗耐药与肿瘤差异和免疫逃逸有关,联合放疗或靶向治疗正在研究。降阶梯仍有争议:RTOG 1016中5年局部区域失败率西妥昔单抗17.3% vs 顺铂9.9%,De-ESCALaTE HPV中2年复发率16.1% vs 6.0%,故符合条件者仍以顺铂为基础CRT为标准。复发/转移HPV阳性HNSCC可获TP53突变(约15%)、KMT2D和PIK3CA突变,提示更侵袭表型和治疗反应降低。 结论:局部晚期HPV阳性HNSCC仍以顺铂为基础CRT为标准,早期和选定低风险患者探索降阶梯,TORS在选定患者有功能获益;复发/转移以全身治疗为主,免疫治疗、靶向治疗和联合策略因毒性担忧而发展;溶瘤病毒、基因治疗、基因编辑和纳米技术等需进一步临床评价。挑战包括无创诊断实施有限、公众认识不足、高成本、缺乏标准化检测、治疗耐药、肿瘤异质性和分子演变,以及免疫治疗患者选择困难。未来应验证可靠生物标志物以改善风险分层,前瞻多中心验证ctHPV DNA并标准化检测和监测间隔,优化降阶梯并识别可安全减量者,将分子谱和NGS整合临床决策。 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! 从2000到2026,27载全因有您;您的每一分支持,都给予我们无穷的动力! 公测期:打赏8元解锁30天免费阅读! 人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)相关头颈癌(HNCs),尤其是口咽鳞状细胞癌(OPSCC),构成日益加重的全球健康负担,近几十年来发病率快速上升。此类肿瘤在生物学和临床上不同于HPV阴性HNCs,更常见于传统危险因素如烟草和酒精暴露有限的年轻个体。HPV驱动的致癌过程由病毒癌蛋白E6和E7介导,其通过使p53和视网膜母细胞瘤(Rb)通路失活破坏基因组稳定性,促进不受控制的增殖、基因组不稳定和治疗耐药。当前HPV阳性HNCs的治疗策略包括手术、放疗和化疗,以顺铂为基础的放化疗(CRT)仍是局部晚期疾病的标准治疗。然而,HPV阳性患者治疗反应和总体预后改善,促使研究人员关注在不损害疗效的前提下降低毒性的治疗降阶梯策略。微创手术方法,如经口机器人手术(TORS),以及降低强度的放疗方案显示出有前景的功能学结局。免疫治疗是复发和转移性疾病的重要进展,靶向PD-1/PD-L1轴的免疫检查点抑制剂在选定患者群体中显示生存获益。新兴方法包括针对HPV癌蛋白的治疗性疫苗、过继性T细胞转移、靶向治疗、溶瘤病毒治疗,以及旨在沉默E6/E7表达或恢复抑癌功能的基因治疗。纳米医学进一步为药物递送、放射增敏和免疫调节提供新平台,提高治疗特异性和疗效。尽管取得显著进展,重大挑战仍然存在,包括早期诊断的限制、治疗耐药、生物标志物驱动的患者选择以及公众对HPV相关癌症风险认识不足。整合先进诊断方法,如循环肿瘤HPV DNA检测和下一代测序(NGS),可能改善风险分层和治疗监测。持续研究联合治疗、靶向方法和患者定制治疗算法对于改善结局仍至关重要。总之,HPV相关HNCs不断演变的治疗策略反映了向精准肿瘤学的转变,重点关注改善生存、降低毒性以及由分子肿瘤特征驱动的个体化干预。 引言:HNCs传统上与吸烟和饮酒相关,但HPV日益成为尤其口咽部恶性肿瘤的重要病因。HPV可经口交、深吻、自体接种和垂直传播;性行为变化和烟草使用下降可能促成HPV相关HNC发病率上升。疾病可在感染后长达40年出现,患者常较年轻、健康且缺乏典型危险因素,导致诊断延迟。HPV阳性HNSCC通常生存优于阴性,但高HPV整合等亚组预后较差。HNC约90%为鳞状细胞癌,2022年全球约74.5万新病例;近几十年HPV相关HNSCC全球发病率增加36.5%,约25% HNC归因于HPV,口咽癌30.8%、喉癌2.4%、口腔癌2.2%;多数与HPV 16/18相关,疫苗是最有效预防手段并应覆盖男性。OPSCC风险分层由NCCN和ESMO共识标准化。本文整合最新降阶梯试验(包括NRG-HN005、ORATOR2、PATHOS)、当前指南推荐、免疫检查点抑制剂更新指征和新兴方法,并评价证据水平与实施障碍。 HPV相关HNCs的流行病学:全球HPV每年导致63万新癌症病例,占4.5%;酒精约5%、烟草34%、二者合并36%的HNC。HPV相关HNSCC发病率上升,危险因素和人口学特征不同于HPV阴性者。HPV相关HNSCC主要发生于口咽,HPV在其他头颈部位因果作用较弱;欧洲新发和死亡数高于美国。HPV阴性HNC多见于老年、社会经济地位较低和口腔卫生差者;HPV阳性者常较年轻(45–64岁)、非吸烟、无明显饮酒史,多个性伴侣尤其口交史为危险因素;男性风险为女性2–4倍,且存在种族差异。分子上HPV阳性肿瘤表达E6/E7并使p53和pRb失活;HPV阴性HNSCC常见TP53和细胞周期调控改变,预后较差。HPV阳性OPSCC放化疗反应和预后优于阴性;HPV在宫颈鳞状细胞癌(CSCC)和OPSCC均关键,但OPSCC放射敏感性更高,口咽局部免疫反应更强,HPV特异性T细胞浸润更多、调节性T细胞(Treg)活性更低。 HPV在癌症发生中的病理机制:WHO将14型HPV列为致癌型。HPV为DNA病毒,嗜鳞状上皮,微损伤使致癌型HPV感染基底上皮干细胞,潜在受体包括整合素α-6、层粘连蛋白-332和硫酸类肝素蛋白聚糖。E1/E2支持病毒复制和附加体维持;E5、E6、E7促进细胞周期进展并抑制凋亡,E4与G2阻滞相关;上层上皮表达L1/L2并组装释放病毒。病毒整合可致突变和染色体异常。HPV通过调节细胞周期、干扰DNA修复、诱导氧化应激和改变端粒长度诱导基因组不稳定;E6促进人端粒酶逆转录酶(hTERT)转录并增加端粒酶活性,延长增殖并延迟衰老。E6结合p53并促其蛋白酶体降解;E7结合pRb使其失活,释放E2F,促进细胞周期基因表达,并可致染色体复制错误和纺锤体异常。E7作为致癌应激激活p53和p16INK4A反应,但E6通过E6相关蛋白(E6AP)介导的泛素-蛋白酶体途径降解p53以抵消保护;二者协同促进永生化与恶性转化。耐药机制包括E6抑制凋亡、E7促进增殖、细胞周期和DNA修复紊乱、干扰Toll样受体(TLRs)等模式识别受体(PRRs)逃避先天免疫、激活DNA损伤反应和修复(DDR)通路,以及缺氧、细胞外基质(ECM)重塑和基质细胞相互作用形成保护性微环境。 HPV相关HNCs的当前治疗策略:历史上HPV阳性和阴性HNSCC治疗相同。局部晚期标准为顺铂为基础CRT,使用70–72 Gy调强放疗(IMRT);单纯放疗用于早期或降阶梯方案。NCCN和EHNS-ESMO-ESTRO将p16阳性口咽癌视为独立实体,AJCC第8版有独立分期;早期推荐根治性放疗或经口手术加颈清扫,局部晚期仍以顺铂为基础CRT为标准;术后结外侵犯或切缘阳性需辅助放疗或放化疗;不推荐西妥昔单抗替代顺铂,临床试验外降阶梯为研究性;复发/转移一线首选依据PD-L1联合阳性评分(CPS)选择的帕博利珠单抗方案。降阶梯试验未证明肿瘤学安全性:RTOG 1016和De-ESCALaTE中西妥昔单抗替代顺铂结局较差且未降低毒性;NRG-HN005中标准CRT 2年无进展生存(PFS)98.1%,减量放疗加顺铂88.6%、加纳武利尤单抗90.3%,均未达非劣效;ORATOR2因手术组两例治疗相关死亡提前终止,2年总生存(OS)放疗100% vs 手术90%,PFS 100% vs 86%。PATHOS相关队列显示TORS后鼻胃管依赖高于经口激光显微手术(TLM)(45.0% vs 7.9%)。TORS在T1–T2且无需辅助治疗时功能获益较明显,需辅助治疗时优势大多消失;TORS加选择性颈清扫(SND)与广泛手术生存相当。IMRT需准确靶区勾画,PET-CT可改变分期和靶区覆盖但缺乏生存和HPV特异性证据;3D打印证据限于小型回顾性系列。复发/转移以铂类联合吉西他滨和顺铂为一线,但疗效有限、毒性高,促使研究新辅助、减量放疗和手术先行。免疫治疗中纳武利尤单抗和帕博利珠单抗靶向PD-1/PD-L1,已用于铂类失败后及一线PD-L1阳性(CPS≥1)或联合铂类和5-氟尿嘧啶;围手术期帕博利珠单抗用于可切除局部晚期HNSCC且CPS≥1。HPV状态不预测免疫治疗获益,单药缓解率约13–19%,获益主要由PD-L1表达决定。治疗性疫苗ISA-101、MEDI0457、PDS0101靶向E6/E7并联合PD-1阻断;过继T细胞转移和工程化TCR在早期研究。NGS可检测PIK3CA、TP53、NOTCH1和表观遗传改变;微滴数字PCR(ddPCR)和循环肿瘤DNA(ctDNA)液体活检用于无创监测。APG-157和组织驻留自然杀伤细胞(trNK)亚群trNK-1等为探索性方向。 新兴治疗策略:许多方法主要由临床前数据支持,细胞系和动物模型不能完全再现人类肿瘤复杂性,需适当期临床试验确认。循环肿瘤HPV DNA(ctHPV DNA)是最有前景的液体活检之一,ddPCR和NGS可检测根治后微小残留病(MRD),可早于影像3–6个月提示复发,但需前瞻多中心验证、标准化方法和截断值。降阶梯旨在减少副作用并保留疗效,策略包括省略化疗、降低或省略放疗,可保留咽喉功能、减少长期毒性、改善生活质量。免疫检查点抑制剂是重要方向,帕博利珠单抗和纳武利尤单抗阻断PD-1/PD-L1,在复发/转移中有效,研究单用或与放化疗联合。靶向治疗包括表皮生长因子受体(EGFR)抑制剂、mTOR和PI3K/Akt通路抑制剂;PI3K抑制剂耐药可被胰岛素样生长因子1受体(IGF1R)抑制剂克服;阿法替尼抑制多个HER受体。溶瘤病毒如T-Vec和Reolysin选择性破坏癌细胞并刺激免疫,在临床试验中与检查点抑制剂联合有潜力。光动力治疗(PDT)用于早期癌症和癌前病变。基因治疗用RNAi、siRNA或shRNA沉默E6/E7;免疫原性基因治疗引入HPV抗原基因;恢复抑癌功能的基因编辑处于实验阶段。纳米颗粒可靶向递送药物、检查点抑制剂和放射增敏剂,降低全身毒性;纳米疫苗如四价纳米疫苗和Qbeta-HPVag在临床前模型增强树突细胞和T细胞活化;ISA101联合纳武利尤单抗II期客观缓解率(ORR)33%、中位OS 17.5个月;磁性纳米颗粒热疗主要在临床前评估。 HPV相关HNCs管理中的挑战:临床评估仍主要依赖侵入性方法,可能延迟诊断;ctHPV DNA液体活检精确但费用高、缺乏标准化。罕见亚型分类需专家病理复核,回顾研究中半数病例复核后重新分类、16%存在重大差异。公众认识不足,调查仅30.6%了解HPV、29.2%将其与口咽癌联系。唾液HPV16 E6/E7检测对p16阳性肿瘤灵敏度72%–77%、特异度90%–94%,但受设备和人员限制。数字健康技术可远程监测症状、体重、营养和毒性,但缺乏HPV相关HNC证据,数据安全和成本待解决。约20–25%HPV阳性HNSCC复发,与肿瘤异质性、免疫逃逸和癌症干细胞样细胞有关;复发癌可见HPV基因活性和染色质结构改变。免疫治疗耐药与肿瘤差异和免疫逃逸有关,联合放疗或靶向治疗正在研究。降阶梯仍有争议:RTOG 1016中5年局部区域失败率西妥昔单抗17.3% vs 顺铂9.9%,De-ESCALaTE HPV中2年复发率16.1% vs 6.0%,故符合条件者仍以顺铂为基础CRT为标准。复发/转移HPV阳性HNSCC可获TP53突变(约15%)、KMT2D和PIK3CA突变,提示更侵袭表型和治疗反应降低。 结论:局部晚期HPV阳性HNSCC仍以顺铂为基础CRT为标准,早期和选定低风险患者探索降阶梯,TORS在选定患者有功能获益;复发/转移以全身治疗为主,免疫治疗、靶向治疗和联合策略因毒性担忧而发展;溶瘤病毒、基因治疗、基因编辑和纳米技术等需进一步临床评价。挑战包括无创诊断实施有限、公众认识不足、高成本、缺乏标准化检测、治疗耐药、肿瘤异质性和分子演变,以及免疫治疗患者选择困难。未来应验证可靠生物标志物以改善风险分层,前瞻多中心验证ctHPV DNA并标准化检测和监测间隔,优化降阶梯并识别可安全减量者,将分子谱和NGS整合临床决策。 打赏 展开全文 开通VIP 享海量文章 全站开放获取+解锁超过 200万篇新闻全文+每日更新 2000+篇,学术前沿动态全时追踪! 从2000到2026,27载全因有您;您的每一分支持,都给予我们无穷的动力! 公测期:打赏8元解锁30天免费阅读! source_language_evidence.scale_impact_and_risk: HPV相关HNCs管理中的挑战:临床评估仍主要依赖侵入性方法,可能延迟诊断;ctHPV DNA液体活检精确但费用高、缺乏标准化。罕见亚型分类需专家病理复核,回顾研究中半数病例复核后重新分类、16%存在重大差异。公众认识不足,调查仅30.6%了解HPV、29.2%将其与口咽癌联系。唾液HPV16 E6/E7检测对p16阳性肿瘤灵敏度72%–77%、特异度90%–94%,但受设备和人员限制。数字健康技术可远程监测症状、体重、营养和毒性,但缺乏HPV相关HNC证据,数据安全和成本待解决。约20–25%HPV阳性HNSCC复发,与肿瘤异质性、免疫逃逸和癌症干细胞样细胞有关;复发癌可见HPV基因活性和染色质结构改变。免疫治疗耐药与肿瘤差异和免疫逃逸有关,联合放疗或靶向治疗正在研究。降阶梯仍有争议:RTOG 1016中5年局部区域失败率西妥昔单抗17.3% vs 顺铂9.9%,De-ESCALaTE HPV中2年复发率16.1% vs 6.0%,故符合条件者仍以顺铂为基础CRT为标准。复发/转移HPV阳性HNSCC可获TP53突变(约15%)、KMT2D和PIK3CA突变,提示更侵袭表型和治疗反应降低。

Advertisement Infections caused about 2.3 million new cancers worldwide in 2024, a global study found. Vaccines, screening and treatment could prevent many of them. About 1 in 8 new cancers diagnosed worldwide in 2024 was caused by an infection, according to a global analysis from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the World Health Organization's cancer research agency. The study, published Sept. 28 in The Lancet Oncology, estimated that infections caused about 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024, or 12% of all new cases. Many of those cancers could be prevented with tools that already exist, including vaccines, screening and treatment for the infections themselves. "The findings underscore the major role that infection control can play in reducing the global cancer burden," Harriet Rumgay, a scientist in IARC's Cancer Surveillance Branch and an author of the study, said in a news release. Which Infections Cause the Most Cancers? Five infections accounted for almost all infection-related cancers, according to IARC: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), a stomach bacterium: about 760,000 cases, mainly stomach cancer Human papillomavirus (HPV): about 750,000 cases, mainly cervical cancer, along with anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and some head and neck cancers Hepatitis B virus: about 360,000 cases, mostly liver cancer Epstein-Barr virus: about 260,000 cases, largely nasopharyngeal cancer (cancer of the upper throat behind the nose), plus some stomach cancers and Hodgkin lymphoma Hepatitis C virus: about 160,000 cases, mostly liver cancer The researchers studied 12 infections known to cause cancer. Their analysis added 16 infection-cancer links that earlier global estimates did not include, among them cancers associated with HIV and with Merkel cell polyomavirus, a virus linked to a rare skin cancer called Merkel cell carcinoma. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up HIV does not cause cancer directly, the National Cancer Institute (NCI) explains, but it raises the risk of several cancers, including Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas and cancers of the cervix, anus, lung, liver and throat. Is Cancer Contagious? No. "A person cannot catch cancer from someone else," according to the American Cancer Society (ACS). What can spread is the infection. Many of the infections that raise cancer risk can pass from person to person, and some can be passed through blood or other body fluids, according to NCI. Infections can lead to cancer in a few ways, the ACS notes. Some viruses directly affect the genes that control how cells grow, some cause long-term inflammation and some weaken the immune system's ability to find and destroy abnormal cells. Even so, most people with these infections never develop cancer. Where Are Infection-Related Cancers Most Common? More than three-quarters of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, according to IARC. Eastern Asia alone accounted for 42% of infection-related cancers worldwide, with a particularly high burden from H. pylori and hepatitis B. Sub-Saharan Africa had very high rates of HPV-related cancers, plus a substantial burden from HIV and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus. IARC said prevention tools are often underused or out of reach, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, because of financial, social and political barriers. How Can Infection-Related Cancers Be Prevented? IARC points to several approaches: Vaccination: Vaccines against HPV and hepatitis B already exist. IARC also called for investment in new vaccines against Epstein-Barr virus, H. pylori and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, for which effective prevention options are not currently available. Screening: Cervical cancer screening is one of the main prevention tools IARC highlighted. Testing and treatment: H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV can be tested for and treated. NCI notes that H. pylori infection can be detected and treated with antibiotics, and recommends seeing a doctor about stomach problems. What Should Patients and Families Ask Their Doctors? If you have questions about HPV vaccination for yourself or your children, testing for hepatitis or H. pylori, or cervical cancer screening, your primary care provider is a good place to start. For people already in cancer treatment, hepatitis B can matter in another way. CURE explains why hepatitis B matters during cancer treatment and who needs testing. Which Infections Cause the Most Cancers? Five infections accounted for almost all infection-related cancers, according to IARC: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), a stomach bacterium: about 760,000 cases, mainly stomach cancer Human papillomavirus (HPV): about 750,000 cases, mainly cervical cancer, along with anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and some head and neck cancers Hepatitis B virus: about 360,000 cases, mostly liver cancer Epstein-Barr virus: about 260,000 cases, largely nasopharyngeal cancer (cancer of the upper throat behind the nose), plus some stomach cancers and Hodgkin lymphoma Hepatitis C virus: about 160,000 cases, mostly liver cancer The researchers studied 12 infections known to cause cancer. Their analysis added 16 infection-cancer links that earlier global estimates did not include, among them cancers associated with HIV and with Merkel cell polyomavirus, a virus linked to a rare skin cancer called Merkel cell carcinoma. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up HIV does not cause cancer directly, the National Cancer Institute (NCI) explains, but it raises the risk of several cancers, including Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas and cancers of the cervix, anus, lung, liver and throat. Is Cancer Contagious? No. "A person cannot catch cancer from someone else," according to the American Cancer Society (ACS). What can spread is the infection. Many of the infections that raise cancer risk can pass from person to person, and some can be passed through blood or other body fluids, according to NCI. Infections can lead to cancer in a few ways, the ACS notes. Some viruses directly affect the genes that control how cells grow, some cause long-term inflammation and some weaken the immune system's ability to find and destroy abnormal cells. Even so, most people with these infections never develop cancer. Where Are Infection-Related Cancers Most Common? More than three-quarters of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, according to IARC. Eastern Asia alone accounted for 42% of infection-related cancers worldwide, with a particularly high burden from H. pylori and hepatitis B. Sub-Saharan Africa had very high rates of HPV-related cancers, plus a substantial burden from HIV and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus. IARC said prevention tools are often underused or out of reach, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, because of financial, social and political barriers. How Can Infection-Related Cancers Be Prevented? IARC points to several approaches: Vaccination: Vaccines against HPV and hepatitis B already exist. IARC also called for investment in new vaccines against Epstein-Barr virus, H. pylori and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, for which effective prevention options are not currently available. Screening: Cervical cancer screening is one of the main prevention tools IARC highlighted. Testing and treatment: H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV can be tested for and treated. NCI notes that H. pylori infection can be detected and treated with antibiotics, and recommends seeing a doctor about stomach problems. What Should Patients and Families Ask Their Doctors? If you have questions about HPV vaccination for yourself or your children, testing for hepatitis or H. pylori, or cervical cancer screening, your primary care provider is a good place to start. For people already in cancer treatment, hepatitis B can matter in another way. CURE explains why hepatitis B matters during cancer treatment and who needs testing. news.content_title: HPV Viral Load Trajectories Predict Cervical Cancer Risk in Prospective
news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer HPV Viral Load Trajectories Predict Cervical Cancer Risk in Prospective Study by November 23, 2026 in Cancer, Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 HPV Viral Load Trajectories Predict Cervical Cancer Risk in Prospective Study Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In a newly published prospective cohort study, researchers report that longitudinal trends in human papillomavirus (HPV) viral load can serve as an informative indicator of cervical cancer risk among women with persistent infections. The findings, published online in CANCER, a peer-reviewed journal of the American Cancer Society, indicate that women exhibiting increasing or persistently high viral-load patterns face a substantially elevated likelihood of developing cervical precancerous lesions compared to those with stable or declining levels. By tracking these viral dynamics over time, clinical teams may gain crucial diagnostic insights that extend well beyond the baseline measurements collected during an initial medical evaluation. While persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus strains has long been recognized as central to the pathogenesis of cervical malignancies, longitudinal changes in viral concentration have remained largely unexamined in clinical research. To address this gap, an investigative team led by researchers at the Changzhou Maternal and Child Health Care Hospital of the Changzhou Medical Center at Nanjing Medical University in China prospectively tracked a cohort of 624 women diagnosed with persistent HPV infections, systematically analyzing their viral measurements across time. Through statistical modeling of the prospective data, the researchers identified four distinct trajectories of viral load among the study participants: low stable, moderate declining, moderate increasing, and persistently high. Evaluating outcomes across these four discrete categories revealed stark disparities in the frequency of cervical abnormalities. Specifically, cervical precancerous lesions developed in 10.9 percent of women within the low stable group and in 17.8 percent of those categorized in the moderate declining group. In sharp contrast, cervical precancerous lesions were identified in 74.2 percent of women in the moderate increasing trajectory and reached 90.4 percent among women exhibiting persistently high viral loads. Discover more Find Cancer Care See an OB-GYN cancer CANCER cancers When comparing relative disease risk across the cohorts, the investigators determined that trajectory patterns were associated with dramatic elevations in the probability of lesion development. Using the low stable trajectory group as the clinical baseline reference, women characterized by a moderate declining viral load exhibited a 1.95-fold higher risk of developing cervical precancerous lesions. For patients with upward or consistently elevated trajectories, the risk escalated sharply, with the moderate increasing group experiencing 29.66 times higher risk and the persistently high trajectory group experiencing an extraordinary 124.29-fold increase in the risk of precancerous lesions relative to the low stable group. Importantly, incorporating longitudinal viral trends directly enhanced clinical risk stratification models. The researchers found that evaluating trajectory patterns substantially improved clinicians’ ability to forecast an individual patient’s risk of developing cervical lesions compared to reliance on conventional predictors alone. While baseline clinical characteristics and initial viral load provide useful starting data, accounting for the direction and trajectory of viral measurements over subsequent visits provided measurable added value in estimating long-term clinical outcomes. The study’s authors emphasized that viral dynamics clarify why individual outcomes can diverge widely among patients who appear clinically comparable upon initial examination. Co-corresponding author Lina Zhang, MD, noted that two women presenting with similar HPV viral loads during a single clinical appointment may ultimately experience very different health trajectories depending entirely on how those concentrations evolve over time. Addressing the broader management of persistent human papillomavirus infections, co-corresponding author Zhonghua Shi, MD, highlighted the clinical imperative to balance vigilance with intervention restraint. A primary obstacle in managing persistent infections has been distinguishing women who genuinely require intensified clinical surveillance from those who can safely avoid redundant or invasive examinations. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health HPV Detected in 91.6% of Respiratory Papillomatosis Patients by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 HPV Detected in 91.6% of Respiratory Papillomatosis Patients Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Infection and Public Health has quantified the global prevalence of human papillomavirus (HPV) in patients with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP). The study, led by Ahmad Adebayo Irekeola and colleagues, synthesized data from 66 distinct studies conducted across diverse geographical and clinical settings. The central finding indicates that HPV was detectable in 91.6% of the 2,214 patients with RRP included in the analysis, establishing a high baseline prevalence of the virus in this rare chronic disorder. This quantitative synthesis addresses a previous gap in the epidemiological literature, providing a standardized measure of HPV detection that complements existing evidence on genotype distribution and disease burden. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is a rare condition characterized by the development of recurrent papillomatous lesions throughout the respiratory tract, with the larynx being the most frequently affected site. Although histologically benign in most cases, the disease can cause substantial morbidity through progressive voice impairment, airway obstruction, and the necessity for repeated surgical interventions. The condition exhibits a bimodal distribution, comprising juvenile-onset RRP (JoRRP) and adult-onset RRP (AoRRP). JoRRP generally presents during childhood and is associated with perinatal acquisition of HPV, whereas AoRRP typically develops in adulthood and is thought to arise from sexual transmission via oral-genital contact. Despite its rarity, RRP imposes a disproportionate clinical burden on patients, families, and healthcare systems due to the need for prolonged and repeated procedures. The pathogenesis of RRP is overwhelmingly associated with low-risk HPV genotypes, particularly types 6 and 11. While other genotypes, including oncogenic types, have occasionally been detected, the predominance of HPV6 and HPV11 distinguishes RRP from many other HPV-associated diseases where high-risk genotypes like HPV16 and HPV18 drive malignant transformation. Understanding the prevalence of HPV infection provides an epidemiological framework for interpreting differences in genotype distribution and clinical presentation. However, previous studies have generally been derived from individual, often small, institution-based populations, providing limited insight into the overall global prevalence of HPV in RRP patients. Discover more Explore Data Book Care Services Find Treatments Find Cancer Care Study Biology To address this gap, the researchers conducted a broad electronic literature search in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect from database inception to March 16, 2026. The search strategy combined terms relating to both the disease and the virus, including “human papillomavirus,” “recurrent respiratory papillomatosis,” and specific subtypes. After screening 3,097 records and removing duplicates, 66 studies met the eligibility criteria for inclusion. These studies were published between 1987 and 2025, with study periods spanning from 1971 to 2021. The majority of the included studies were retrospective in design, representing diverse geographical settings across Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania, and South America. The meta-analysis employed a random-effects model based on the DerSimonian–Laird method to calculate pooled estimates, anticipating considerable clinical, geographical, and methodological heterogeneity. The primary outcome was the prevalence of HPV in patients with RRP, defined as the proportion of patients who tested positive for HPV among those assessed. Secondary outcomes included the prevalence of specific HPV genotypes, particularly HPV6 and HPV11. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data. Given a minimum overall score of 77.8%, the studies were classified as having a low risk of bias, ensuring a robust foundation for the quantitative synthesis. The pooled prevalence of HPV among all patients with RRP, irrespective of subtype, was 91.6% (95% CI: 88.2–94.2). Considerable between-study heterogeneity was observed, with an I2 statistic of 76.2%. To assess the robustness of this estimate, the researchers performed leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, which showed that the pooled prevalence ranged only from 91.4% to 92.1% following the sequential exclusion of individual studies. This stability indicates that no single study substantially altered the overall pooled estimate, reinforcing the consistency of HPV detection across the included populations. Subgroup analyses revealed variations in HPV prevalence across different geographical regions and study periods. The highest prevalence was observed in North America at 94.2%, followed by Oceania at 93.2% and South America at 92.6%. The lowest pooled prevalence was found in Asia at 86.6%. When stratified by study period, studies conducted from 2015 onwards showed a higher pooled prevalence of 94.6% compared to 88.5% for studies conducted before 2015. The authors caution that this temporal difference may reflect methodological variations or differences in population characteristics rather than a genuine increase in HPV prevalence, as diagnostic methods and study designs varied across the included literature. Discover more Read Med Journals Find ENT Doctors Find Lung Care Book a Checkup Check Symptoms Genotype-specific analyses demonstrated substantial differences in the distribution of HPV6 and HPV11. HPV6 was detected in 61.1% of patients across 52 studies, whereas HPV11 was detected in 41.2% across 49 studies. These genotypes also showed different patterns according to RRP subtype. In patients with JoRRP, the pooled prevalence of any HPV was 94.7%, with HPV6 detected in 58.6% and HPV11 in 50.2%. In contrast, among patients with AoRRP, the pooled prevalence of any HPV was 86.5%, with HPV6 detected in 68.1% and HPV11 in 32.9%. The higher prevalence of HPV11 in JoRRP is consistent with previous observations linking this genotype to younger age at diagnosis and potentially more aggressive disease characteristics. The study also examined the impact of specimen type on HPV detection rates. Studies using invasive specimens, such as tissue biopsies, demonstrated a pooled HPV prevalence of 92.2%. In comparison, studies using non-invasive or minimally invasive specimens, such as saliva or oral rinses, showed a lower pooled prevalence of 82.9%. This difference is methodologically plausible, as tissue obtained directly from papillomatous lesions provides the most direct evidence of HPV infection within the disease site. HPV detected in oral fluids may vary according to disease activity and viral shedding, and cannot invariably be assumed to originate from the RRP lesion itself. Assessment of publication bias using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test indicated significant asymmetry, suggesting the possibility of small-study effects. Following the application of the trim-and-fill procedure, the adjusted pooled prevalence was 87.1% (95% CI: 82.7–90.6). While this adjustment accounts for potentially missing studies, the authors note that this method relies on assumptions that may not fully account for the substantial heterogeneity inherent to prevalence meta-analyses. Therefore, the adjusted estimate should be interpreted as a sensitivity measure rather than a definitive correction of the primary finding. The study has several strengths, including the incorporation of evidence from 66 studies spanning several decades and multiple geographical regions. The study, led by Ahmad Adebayo Irekeola and colleagues, synthesized data from 66 distinct studies conducted across diverse geographical and clinical settings. The central finding indicates that HPV was detectable in 91.6% of the 2,214 patients with RRP included in the analysis, establishing a high baseline prevalence of the virus in this rare chronic disorder. This quantitative synthesis addresses a previous gap in the epidemiological literature, providing a standardized measure of HPV detection that complements existing evidence on genotype distribution and disease burden. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is a rare condition characterized by the development of recurrent papillomatous lesions throughout the respiratory tract, with the larynx being the most frequently affected site. Although histologically benign in most cases, the disease can cause substantial morbidity through progressive voice impairment, airway obstruction, and the necessity for repeated surgical interventions. The condition exhibits a bimodal distribution, comprising juvenile-onset RRP (JoRRP) and adult-onset RRP (AoRRP). JoRRP generally presents during childhood and is associated with perinatal acquisition of HPV, whereas AoRRP typically develops in adulthood and is thought to arise from sexual transmission via oral-genital contact. Despite its rarity, RRP imposes a disproportionate clinical burden on patients, families, and healthcare systems due to the need for prolonged and repeated procedures. The pathogenesis of RRP is overwhelmingly associated with low-risk HPV genotypes, particularly types 6 and 11. While other genotypes, including oncogenic types, have occasionally been detected, the predominance of HPV6 and HPV11 distinguishes RRP from many other HPV-associated diseases where high-risk genotypes like HPV16 and HPV18 drive malignant transformation. Understanding the prevalence of HPV infection provides an epidemiological framework for interpreting differences in genotype distribution and clinical presentation. However, previous studies have generally been derived from individual, often small, institution-based populations, providing limited insight into the overall global prevalence of HPV in RRP patients. Discover more Explore Data Book Care Services Find Treatments Find Cancer Care Study Biology To address this gap, the researchers conducted a broad electronic literature search in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect from database inception to March 16, 2026. The search strategy combined terms relating to both the disease and the virus, including “human papillomavirus,” “recurrent respiratory papillomatosis,” and specific subtypes. After screening 3,097 records and removing duplicates, 66 studies met the eligibility criteria for inclusion. These studies were published between 1987 and 2025, with study periods spanning from 1971 to 2021. The majority of the included studies were retrospective in design, representing diverse geographical settings across Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania, and South America. The meta-analysis employed a random-effects model based on the DerSimonian–Laird method to calculate pooled estimates, anticipating considerable clinical, geographical, and methodological heterogeneity. The primary outcome was the prevalence of HPV in patients with RRP, defined as the proportion of patients who tested positive for HPV among those assessed. Secondary outcomes included the prevalence of specific HPV genotypes, particularly HPV6 and HPV11. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data. Given a minimum overall score of 77.8%, the studies were classified as having a low risk of bias, ensuring a robust foundation for the quantitative synthesis. The pooled prevalence of HPV among all patients with RRP, irrespective of subtype, was 91.6% (95% CI: 88.2–94.2). Considerable between-study heterogeneity was observed, with an I2 statistic of 76.2%. To assess the robustness of this estimate, the researchers performed leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, which showed that the pooled prevalence ranged only from 91.4% to 92.1% following the sequential exclusion of individual studies. This stability indicates that no single study substantially altered the overall pooled estimate, reinforcing the consistency of HPV detection across the included populations. Subgroup analyses revealed variations in HPV prevalence across different geographical regions and study periods. The highest prevalence was observed in North America at 94.2%, followed by Oceania at 93.2% and South America at 92.6%. The lowest pooled prevalence was found in Asia at 86.6%. When stratified by study period, studies conducted from 2015 onwards showed a higher pooled prevalence of 94.6% compared to 88.5% for studies conducted before 2015. The authors caution that this temporal difference may reflect methodological variations or differences in population characteristics rather than a genuine increase in HPV prevalence, as diagnostic methods and study designs varied across the included literature. Discover more Read Med Journals Find ENT Doctors Find Lung Care Book a Checkup Check Symptoms Genotype-specific analyses demonstrated substantial differences in the distribution of HPV6 and HPV11. HPV6 was detected in 61.1% of patients across 52 studies, whereas HPV11 was detected in 41.2% across 49 studies. These genotypes also showed different patterns according to RRP subtype. In patients with JoRRP, the pooled prevalence of any HPV was 94.7%, with HPV6 detected in 58.6% and HPV11 in 50.2%. In contrast, among patients with AoRRP, the pooled prevalence of any HPV was 86.5%, with HPV6 detected in 68.1% and HPV11 in 32.9%. The higher prevalence of HPV11 in JoRRP is consistent with previous observations linking this genotype to younger age at diagnosis and potentially more aggressive disease characteristics. The study also examined the impact of specimen type on HPV detection rates. Studies using invasive specimens, such as tissue biopsies, demonstrated a pooled HPV prevalence of 92.2%. In comparison, studies using non-invasive or minimally invasive specimens, such as saliva or oral rinses, showed a lower pooled prevalence of 82.9%. This difference is methodologically plausible, as tissue obtained directly from papillomatous lesions provides the most direct evidence of HPV infection within the disease site. HPV detected in oral fluids may vary according to disease activity and viral shedding, and cannot invariably be assumed to originate from the RRP lesion itself. Assessment of publication bias using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test indicated significant asymmetry, suggesting the possibility of small-study effects. Following the application of the trim-and-fill procedure, the adjusted pooled prevalence was 87.1% (95% CI: 82.7–90.6). While this adjustment accounts for potentially missing studies, the authors note that this method relies on assumptions that may not fully account for the substantial heterogeneity inherent to prevalence meta-analyses. Therefore, the adjusted estimate should be interpreted as a sensitivity measure rather than a definitive correction of the primary finding. The study has several strengths, including the incorporation of evidence from 66 studies spanning several decades and multiple geographical regions. The stability of the overall estimate in sensitivity analyses strengthens confidence that the principal finding was not driven by a single influential study. However, limitations include the limited number of studies in some geographical and methodological subgroups, which restricts the precision of their corresponding estimates. Additionally, individual-level factors such as vaccination history, disease duration, and immune status could not be consistently examined due to the reliance on aggregate published data. The findings reinforce the central epidemiological role of HPV in RRP and provide a global quantitative benchmark for future epidemiological and vaccine-impact studies. The observed high prevalence across diverse settings supports the interpretation of RRP as a predominantly HPV-associated disease across the lifespan. Continued surveillance using incident RRP cases, individual vaccination histories, and standardized HPV detection methods will be critical for determining whether increasing vaccination coverage translates into sustained reductions in HPV-associated RRP and for clarifying the longer-term epidemiological impact of prevention programs.
